title: UNIT 1: ATOMIC STRUCTURE AND PERIODIC PROPERTIES OF THE ELEMENTS
notes: ✓ Atomic structure → Explains the composition of atoms, the behavior of electrons, and how electrons are arranged around the nucleus.

title: 1.1 Introduction
notes:
✓ Atom → The smallest unit of an element that retains the chemical identity of that element.
Atoms are made of a small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons.

The modern understanding of the atom developed through experiments and theories. Early ideas treated atoms as indivisible particles, but later discoveries showed that atoms contain smaller subatomic particles and have complex internal structures.

title: 1.2 Dalton’s Atomic Theory and Modern Atomic Theory
notes:
✓ John Dalton developed an atomic theory to explain the laws of chemical combination. Later experimental discoveries showed that some of Dalton’s ideas needed modification.

✓ Modern atomic theory → Recognizes that atoms contain subatomic particles, atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons, and atoms can be changed in nuclear processes.

→ The modern view preserves the important idea that matter is composed of atoms while incorporating the discoveries of electrons, protons, neutrons, isotopes, and nuclear structure.

title: 1.2.1 Postulates of Dalton’s Atomic Theory
notes:
✓ Dalton proposed that:
◆ Matter is composed of very small particles called atoms.
◆ Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties.
◆ Atoms of different elements have different masses and properties.
◆ Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
◆ Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in ordinary chemical reactions; they are rearranged.

→ Some of these ideas were later modified. Atoms contain smaller particles, isotopes of the same element can have different masses, and atoms can undergo changes in nuclear reactions.

title: 1.2.2 Postulates of Modern Atomic Theory
notes:
✓ Modern atomic theory → Matter is composed of atoms containing subatomic particles.
Atoms of the same element have the same number of protons but may have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses.

✓ Atoms combine in whole-number ratios to form compounds, and chemical reactions involve rearrangement of atoms.

✓ Atomic number → The number of protons in the nucleus, which determines the identity of an element.

→ Nuclear reactions can change one element into another, showing that atoms are not absolutely indivisible.

title: 1.3 Early Experiments to Characterize the Atom
notes:
✓ Experiments involving electricity, cathode rays, radioactivity, and particle scattering provided evidence that atoms contain smaller particles and a central nucleus.

◆ IMPORTANT DISCOVERIES
✓ Electron.
✓ Atomic nucleus.
✓ Neutron.

→ These discoveries changed the model of the atom from an indivisible particle to a structure containing a small nucleus surrounded by electrons.

title: 1.3.1 Discovery of the Electron
notes:
✓ Electron → A negatively charged subatomic particle present in atoms of different elements.

✓ Cathode rays → Were shown to consist of negatively charged particles.

✓ J. J. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of these particles and concluded that electrons are much smaller than atoms.

✓ Electron → Has a negative charge and a very small mass compared with protons and neutrons.

→ The discovery of the electron demonstrated that atoms are divisible and contain negatively charged subatomic particles.

title: 1.3.2 Radioactivity and Discovery of the Nucleus
notes:
✓ Radioactivity → The spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable atomic nuclei.

◆ TYPES OF RADIOACTIVE RADIATION
✓ Alpha (α).
✓ Beta (β).
✓ Gamma (γ).

✓ Rutherford’s scattering experiment → Most alpha particles passed through thin metal foil with little or no deflection, while a small number were strongly deflected.

◆ RUTHERFORD'S CONCLUSIONS
✓ Most of the atom is empty space.
✓ Nearly all the positive charge is concentrated in a very small region.
✓ Most of the atom’s mass is concentrated in this region.

→ Nucleus → The small, dense central region of the atom.

title: 1.3.3 Discovery of the Neutron
notes:
✓ Neutron → A subatomic particle with approximately the same mass as a proton but with no electrical charge.

✓ James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 through experiments involving radiation produced when alpha particles interacted with beryllium.

→ The discovery of the neutron explained why atomic nuclei have greater masses than could be accounted for by protons alone and helped explain the existence of isotopes.

title: 1.4 Make-up of the Nucleus
notes:
✓ Nucleus → The small, dense central region of an atom containing positively charged protons and electrically neutral neutrons.

✓ Almost all of the atom’s mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

✓ Number of protons → Determines the identity of an element.
✓ Mass number → Total number of protons and neutrons.

→ Electrons occupy the region surrounding the nucleus and have a very small mass compared with nuclear particles.

title: 1.4.1 Subatomic Particles
notes:
✓ The three major subatomic particles are electrons, protons, and neutrons.

◆ ELECTRON
✓ Charge = −1.
✓ Located outside the nucleus.
✓ Very small mass.

◆ PROTON
✓ Charge = +1.
✓ Located in the nucleus.
✓ Mass ≈ 1 atomic mass unit.

◆ NEUTRON
✓ Charge = 0.
✓ Located in the nucleus.
✓ Mass ≈ 1 atomic mass unit.

✓ Atomic number (Z) → Number of protons.
✓ In a neutral atom → Number of electrons = Number of protons.
✓ Mass number (A) → Number of protons + Number of neutrons.

title: 1.4.2 Atomic Mass and Isotopes
notes:
✓ Isotopes → Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

→ Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

✓ Example: Carbon has isotopes such as carbon-12, carbon-13, and carbon-14. Each contains six protons but a different number of neutrons.

✓ Average atomic mass → Generally a weighted average of the masses of the naturally occurring isotopes of an element.

✓ Average atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × fractional abundance).

title: 1.5 Electromagnetic Radiation and Atomic Spectra
notes:
✓ Electromagnetic radiation → Energy that travels through space as oscillating electric and magnetic fields.

◆ ELECTROMAGNETIC RADIATION INCLUDES
✓ Radio waves.
✓ Microwaves.
✓ Infrared radiation.
✓ Visible light.
✓ Ultraviolet radiation.
✓ X-rays.
✓ Gamma rays.

→ Atoms can absorb or emit electromagnetic radiation. The resulting atomic spectra provide evidence that electrons have specific allowed energy states.

title: 1.5.1 Electromagnetic Radiation
notes:
✓ Wavelength (λ) → The distance between corresponding points on successive waves.
✓ Frequency (ν) → The number of waves passing a point per second.

✓ Speed of light:
c = λν

✓ c → Speed of light.

→ Electromagnetic radiation is arranged in the electromagnetic spectrum according to wavelength or frequency.
→ Shorter wavelength → Higher frequency → Higher photon energy.

title: 1.5.2 Quantum Theory and Photon
notes:
✓ Max Planck proposed that electromagnetic energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete amounts called quanta.

✓ Einstein described light as consisting of packets of energy called photons.

✓ Photon energy:
E = hν

✓ Since c = λν:
E = hc/λ

→ High-frequency radiation → Greater photon energy.
→ Long-wavelength radiation → Lower photon energy.

title: 1.5.3 Atomic Spectra
notes:
✓ When atoms absorb or emit energy, electrons can move between allowed energy levels. The emitted or absorbed radiation produces characteristic spectral lines.

◆ EMISSION SPECTRUM
✓ Produced when excited atoms release energy as light.

◆ ABSORPTION SPECTRUM
✓ Occurs when atoms absorb specific wavelengths from continuous radiation.

→ Each element has a characteristic spectrum because its electrons have specific allowed energy differences.
→ Atomic spectra provide information about the internal energy structure of atoms.

title: 1.5.4 Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
notes:
✓ Niels Bohr proposed a model in which the electron in a hydrogen atom can occupy only certain allowed energy levels.

◆ BOHR MODEL
✓ Electrons occupy specific energy levels or orbits.
✓ Electrons in an allowed orbit do not continuously lose energy.
✓ Energy is absorbed when an electron moves to a higher energy level.
✓ Energy is emitted when an electron moves to a lower energy level.

✓ Energy change:
ΔE = hν

→ The Bohr model successfully explained the line spectrum of hydrogen.

title: 1.5.5 Limitations of the Bohr Model
notes:
✓ The Bohr model successfully explains the hydrogen spectrum but has important limitations.

→ It cannot adequately explain the spectra of atoms containing more than one electron.
→ It does not fully account for the detailed behavior of electrons, including their wave-like nature and the effects described by modern quantum mechanics.

✓ Modern quantum mechanical model → Provides a more complete description of electrons in atoms.

title: 1.5.6 Wave-Particle Duality of Matter and Energy
notes:
✓ Electromagnetic radiation shows both wave-like and particle-like behavior.

→ Light behaves as a wave during phenomena such as interference and diffraction, while photons demonstrate its particle nature.

✓ Louis de Broglie proposed that matter particles such as electrons can also have wave-like properties.

✓ de Broglie wavelength:
λ = h/mv

→ This idea helped establish the quantum mechanical description of the atom.

title: 1.6 Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
notes:
✓ Quantum mechanical model → Describes electrons using mathematical probability rather than fixed circular paths.

✓ Wave function → Mathematical description of an electron's state.
✓ Atomic orbital → Region where there is a high probability of finding an electron.

→ Unlike the Bohr model, electrons are not assumed to travel in definite circular orbits around the nucleus.

✓ Quantum numbers → Describe the energy, size, shape, and orientation of orbitals.

title: 1.6.1 Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle
notes:
✓ Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle → It is impossible to know the exact position and exact momentum of an electron simultaneously.

→ The more precisely the position of an electron is known, the less precisely its momentum can be known, and vice versa.

→ Electrons cannot be described as moving in precise fixed paths. Instead, their positions are described in terms of probability.

title: 1.6.2 Quantum Numbers
notes:
✓ Quantum numbers → Used to describe the state of an electron in an atom.

◆ PRINCIPAL QUANTUM NUMBER (n)
✓ Describes the main energy level or shell.
✓ Values → 1, 2, 3, ...
→ Larger n generally corresponds to greater energy and greater average distance from the nucleus.

◆ AZIMUTHAL QUANTUM NUMBER (l)
✓ Describes the subshell and orbital shape.
✓ For a given n, l can have values from 0 to n−1.
→ Values correspond to s, p, d, and f subshells.

◆ MAGNETIC QUANTUM NUMBER (mₗ)
✓ Describes the orientation of an orbital.
✓ Values → −l to +l.

◆ SPIN QUANTUM NUMBER (mₛ)
✓ Describes electron spin.
✓ Values → +1/2 or −1/2.

→ These four quantum numbers provide a complete description of an electron in an atom.

title: 1.6.3 Shapes of Atomic Orbitals
notes:
✓ Atomic orbital → Region around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron.

◆ s ORBITALS
✓ Spherical shape.
✓ One orbital.
✓ Maximum of two electrons.

◆ p ORBITALS
✓ Dumbbell-shaped orbitals.
✓ Three orbitals.
✓ Maximum of six electrons.

◆ d ORBITALS
✓ Five orbitals.
✓ Maximum of ten electrons.
✓ Many d orbitals have more complex shapes.

◆ f ORBITALS
✓ Seven orbitals.
✓ Maximum of fourteen electrons.

→ The maximum number of electrons in a subshell depends on the number of orbitals it contains.

title: 1.7 Electronic Configurations and Orbital Diagrams
notes:
✓ Electronic configuration → Describes how electrons are distributed among the shells, subshells, and orbitals of an atom.

✓ Electrons occupy orbitals according to their relative energies.

◆ AUFBAU PRINCIPLE
✓ Electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.

◆ PAULI EXCLUSION PRINCIPLE
✓ An orbital can contain a maximum of two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.

◆ HUND’S RULE
✓ When electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy, they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing.

→ Orbital diagrams use boxes or lines for orbitals and arrows for electrons.

title: 1.7.1 Ground State Electronic Configuration
notes:
✓ Ground-state electronic configuration → Arrangement of electrons in the lowest available energy state of an atom.

✓ Common filling order:
1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p → 7s ...

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Hydrogen → 1s¹
✓ Helium → 1s²
✓ Carbon → 1s² 2s² 2p²
✓ Oxygen → 1s² 2s² 2p⁴
✓ Sodium → 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹

→ For a neutral atom, the number of electrons in the configuration must equal the atomic number.

title: 1.8 Electronic Configurations and the Periodic Table
notes:
✓ Electron configuration → Closely related to an element's position in the periodic table.

✓ Highest occupied principal energy level → Helps identify the period.
✓ Valence-electron arrangement → Helps explain the group and chemical behavior.

→ The periodic table is organized according to increasing atomic number, and elements with similar outer-electron configurations show similar chemical properties.

◆ BLOCKS OF THE PERIODIC TABLE
✓ s-block.
✓ p-block.
✓ d-block.
✓ f-block.

→ Blocks are classified according to the subshell being filled.

title: 1.8.1 The Modern Periodic Table
notes:
✓ Modern periodic table → Arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number.

✓ Periods → Horizontal rows.
✓ Groups → Vertical columns.

→ Elements in the same group generally have related valence-electron configurations and similar chemical properties.

◆ CLASSIFICATION
✓ Metals.
✓ Nonmetals.
✓ Metalloids.
✓ Representative elements.
✓ Transition elements.
✓ Inner-transition elements.

title: 1.8.2 Classification of the Elements
notes:
✓ Elements can be classified according to their electron configurations and positions in the periodic table.

◆ REPRESENTATIVE ELEMENTS
✓ Main-group elements in the s and p blocks.

◆ TRANSITION ELEMENTS
✓ Elements associated mainly with the d block, where d subshells are being filled.

◆ INNER-TRANSITION ELEMENTS
✓ Lanthanides and actinides, associated with filling f subshells.

◆ BROAD CLASSIFICATION
✓ Metals.
✓ Nonmetals.
✓ Metalloids.

→ These classifications are based on the physical and chemical properties and electronic configurations of the elements.

title: 1.8.3 Periodic Properties
notes:
✓ Periodic properties → Properties that show regular trends as atomic number increases across periods and down groups.

◆ ATOMIC RADIUS
✓ Generally decreases from left to right across a period.
✓ Generally increases down a group.

◆ IONIZATION ENERGY
✓ Generally increases from left to right across a period.
✓ Generally decreases down a group.

◆ ELECTRON AFFINITY
✓ Generally becomes more favorable across a period, although the trend has exceptions.

◆ ELECTRONEGATIVITY
✓ Generally increases from left to right across a period.
✓ Generally decreases down a group.
✓ Fluorine has the highest electronegativity.

◆ METALLIC CHARACTER
✓ Generally decreases from left to right across a period.
✓ Generally increases down a group.

→ These trends are related mainly to nuclear charge, electron shielding, and distance between the nucleus and outer electrons.

title: 1.8.4 Advantages of Periodic Classification
notes:
✓ Periodic classification → Provides a systematic way to organize and study the elements.

◆ IMPORTANT ADVANTAGES
✓ Classification is based on atomic number, a fundamental property of an element.
✓ Isotopes of an element occupy the same position because they have the same atomic number.
✓ Periodic trends can be related to electronic configurations.
✓ Anomalous pairs such as argon and potassium are correctly placed according to atomic number.
✓ Lanthanides and actinides can be displayed separately at the bottom of the table.
✓ The table provides a simple and systematic way to study and predict the properties of elements.

→ The position of an element can therefore provide useful information about its electronic configuration and chemical behavior.

title: UNIT 1 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ ATOM → Smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity.

✓ ATOMIC NUMBER (Z) → Number of protons.
✓ MASS NUMBER (A) → Protons + neutrons.
✓ ISOTOPES → Same element, same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons.

✓ ELECTRON → Negative charge.
✓ PROTON → Positive charge.
✓ NEUTRON → No charge.

✓ c = λν
✓ E = hν = hc/λ
✓ λ = h/mv

✓ BOHR MODEL → Electrons occupy specific energy levels and emit or absorb energy when moving between them.
✓ QUANTUM MECHANICAL MODEL → Electrons are described by probability distributions called orbitals.
✓ QUANTUM NUMBERS → n, l, mₗ, mₛ.

✓ AUFBAU → Fill lower-energy orbitals first.
✓ PAULI → Maximum two electrons per orbital with opposite spins.
✓ HUND → Equal-energy orbitals are singly occupied before pairing.

◆ SUBSHELL CAPACITIES
✓ s → 1 orbital → 2 electrons.
✓ p → 3 orbitals → 6 electrons.
✓ d → 5 orbitals → 10 electrons.
✓ f → 7 orbitals → 14 electrons.

✓ PERIODIC TABLE → Elements arranged according to increasing atomic number.

✓ ATOMIC RADIUS → Generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
✓ IONIZATION ENERGY → Generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
✓ ELECTRONEGATIVITY → Generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
✓ METALLIC CHARACTER → Generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
